The product

Meet Solvere. Turn it around.

A Room pod in every room she uses, a hub, and a bedside pod. They notice a fall or a quiet change, ask if she's okay right there in the room, and send a real person when she needs one. No cameras. Nothing to wear. Nothing she has to charge. The same devices work in a care home.

Power

Always on. Low voltage only.

A radar that must never miss a fall is on all the time: 12 to 34 Wh a day on Seeed's kit (0.5 to 1.4 W). A battery alone would soon run down. So each device takes 5 V from the nearest outlet through a thin USB-C cable, and carries a battery for power outages and for rooms with no outlet. No wall voltage inside any Solvere device.

Every room

Every room she uses. No blind spots.

Falls happen all over the house, so each room she uses gets a Room pod, mounted where a radar can actually see the floor.

Eye level, not outlet level

Wall outlets sit low, behind beds and sofas, and we found no product that detects falls from there. Vayyar's Walabot shipped radar fall detection mounted on the wall at about 1.5 m. The Room pod goes there too: reached standing, no ladder.

A radar that sees height

A 3D radar tells standing from lying on the floor. With a wide vertical view it reaches the floor from about 0.9 m out. TI's own wall-mounted fall demo uses this class of radar.

Buy by the room

The starter kit covers three rooms: bathroom, bedroom and living room. Add a pod for each extra room she uses. A five-bedroom house doesn't need five pods if she lives in three rooms.

Last seen, never lost

If she walks into a room with no pod and doesn't come out in her usual time, the nearest pod asks "Are you okay?", then family is told. Try it in the demo below.

Care homes use the same pod, mounted at 2.2 to 2.5 m on a 20° plate. TI recommends mounting above 2 m and tilting more than 20° down for tall wall mounts.

Setup

Nobody climbs. Nobody pairs. Nobody maps.

Radar sensors today can take days of mapping rooms by hand, and care-home rollouts stall on old Wi-Fi. We designed both problems out.

      She's in charge

      Things she can say

        Consent

        She agrees in her own words.

        At setup the hub explains what it does and asks her. If dementia means she can't decide, her legal proxy (power of attorney or healthcare proxy) does, and it's recorded. She can change what's shared any time.

        The safety net

        From a fall to a person at the door.

        Fixed rules decide every step, not AI. Each step has a clock. If nobody answers, the next step starts on its own.

          What 911 receives

          Possible fall · no answerUrgent
          Where
          12 Maple Ct, Apt 4 · bathroom
          What
          Fall at 2:21 am, no movement, asked twice
          Her notes
          81 · type 2 diabetes · blood thinner
          Door
          One-time code 4 8 1 9 · valid 30 min
          Sample data. Sent through a 911 data partner (RapidSOS-type link).

          Getting in

          The door is locked. She's on the floor.

          A smart lock or key lockbox. A one-time code goes only to the person who accepted, lasts 30 minutes, and is logged. She agrees to this at setup.

          Talk to her

          "Mom, Asha is 4 minutes away."

          Family or the responder can speak through the device nearest to her, so she's never alone on the floor wondering if anyone knows.

          Always connected

          Works with no internet, no Wi-Fi and no power.

          The safety path never depends on the family's router or the cloud. Decisions happen inside the home.

            Care homes

            Built for the building, not bolted on.

            Assisted living, memory care and nursing homes. In a typical 100-bed nursing home, 100 to 200 falls are reported every year, and half to three-quarters of residents fall (CDC). Same Room pods, mounted high by facilities, on the building's own power and our own network.

            Solvere Intelligence

            Our own AI. It gets better with every home.

            Not a borrowed voice assistant. One agent, built end to end for older adults, from the radar signal to the words she hears.

            Worldwide

            One device. Every tier-one market.

            We launch in the US first. The hardware is designed from day one to ship to Canada, the UK, Europe and the Nordics, the Gulf, and Australia and New Zealand.

            What's real today

            • 3D designs for every device (Room pod with its home and care-home plates, hub, bedside pod, tags), checked in code: zero overlaps between parts.
            • Radar windows 1.47 mm thick with a 2.5 mm air gap, from Seeed's own radome formula.
            • The coverage geometry: eye level sees the floor from 0.9 m, and where furniture hides it.
            • A printable enclosure for Seeed's radar kit, for bench tests now.
            • This app, care console, simulator and 3D studio as clickable prototypes.

            What's still ahead

            • Choose the 3D radar module, then prove eye-level fall detection against a ceiling pod, with real furniture.
            • Partners to sign: monitoring centers (US, UK, EU), 911 data, eSIM carrier, glucose data, nurse call and EHR.
            • Certification per market (FCC, CE, UKCA and more) and measured battery life.
            • Times like "help in 7 minutes" are examples, not promises yet.

            Who pays

            Five ways in.

            Families

            A monthly plan for a parent living on their own: the devices, the app, and a person who comes.

            Care homes

            Per bed. Every room looked after without cameras, and staff sent to the right door first.

            Medicaid waivers

            48 states and DC already pay for emergency response systems through home care waivers: typically $25 to $75 a month, plus setup.

            Health programs

            Medicare's ACCESS model pays $90 to $420 per patient per year for better chronic care. Our cuff and glucose trends fit it.

            Public telecare

            UK councils and European municipalities already fund alarm services for older people at home. We speak their digital alarm protocols.
